Copper price outlook 2026: energy transition and the structural deficit

Goldman Sachs projects copper in a $10,000–$11,000 per tonne range through 2026 and 2027. The reason is not a demand spike — it is a decade-long structural story about where the world gets its electricity and why the mines cannot keep up.

Where copper stands in October 2026

Copper has been one of the more closely watched industrial metals of 2026. After trading around $8,500–$9,000 per metric tonne through much of 2024, the price has pushed higher as the pace of electrification investments accelerated globally and a handful of supply disruptions in South America tightened the physical market. Goldman Sachs now expects the price to hold in a $10,000–$11,000 per metric tonne band for the rest of 2026 and into 2027 — a view aligned with what BMI (Business Monitor International) and other commodity research houses have been saying: demand growth is real and supply growth is not keeping up.

For context, a copper price near $10,000 per tonne translates to roughly $4.54 per pound on U.S. futures markets. That is well above the marginal cost of production for most mines, which means the high price is not a manufacturing quirk — it reflects a genuine imbalance between how much copper the world is consuming and how much is being produced.

Why the energy transition is the dominant demand story

Copper has always been essential for electricity — it is the workhorse conductor, cheap enough to use at scale and efficient enough to justify almost everywhere. But the energy transition has dramatically expanded the addressable market for copper in ways that are still working their way through the data.

Electric vehicles are the most-cited example, and for good reason. A typical internal combustion engine car uses roughly 20 kilograms of copper across its wiring, motors and heat exchangers. An electric vehicle uses between 80 and 100 kilograms — four to five times as much. As the share of EVs in new vehicle sales continues to rise worldwide, each percentage point of adoption is an incremental demand signal that would not have existed a decade ago.

Solar power is the second major driver. A utility-scale solar installation requires approximately 5.5 tonnes of copper per megawatt of generating capacity — in the cells, inverters, cabling and grid connections. Offshore wind is even more intensive at roughly 10 tonnes per megawatt, partly because subsea cables are expensive to maintain and therefore over-engineered from the start. Governments across Europe, North America and Asia have committed to significant renewable capacity additions through 2030, and copper threads through virtually every megawatt of that build-out.

Grid modernization adds another layer. Aging transmission infrastructure in developed markets needs replacement, and newer grid architectures designed for distributed generation and two-way power flows are inherently more copper-intensive than the simple hub-and-spoke grids they replace. The rise of large data center clusters — fuelled by AI infrastructure spending — is also adding to demand; a modern hyperscale data center is, among other things, a substantial consumer of copper in its power distribution and cooling systems.

Taken together, these demand drivers are structural rather than cyclical. They do not go away in a recession the way steel demand might soften when construction slows. The electrification build-out is happening across economic cycles, underwritten by government policy commitments and corporate capital expenditure plans locked in years in advance.

The supply problem copper faces

The challenge for the copper market is that supply cannot ramp up quickly in response to higher prices — and this is a feature of the industry, not a failure. Opening a major new copper mine today takes, on average, fifteen to twenty years from initial discovery through feasibility study, permitting, construction and ramp-up to full production. That timeline means the decisions made today about which deposits to develop will determine supply availability in the 2040s, not the late 2020s.

In the meantime, the deposits currently in production are getting harder to work. Ore grades — the concentration of copper in the rock — have been declining at many of the world's largest mines over the past two decades. Processing lower-grade ore requires more energy and more water, and produces more tailings waste per tonne of copper recovered. Unit costs rise even as output is maintained. Chile and Peru, which together account for roughly 40% of global mined copper supply, have also seen operational disruptions from community protests, water scarcity and regulatory changes that have added uncertainty to output forecasts.

This is the backdrop against which analysts arrive at their supply-deficit projections. The International Energy Agency, BloombergNEF and several investment banks have at various points modelled scenarios in which copper demand outstrips supply sometime between 2026 and 2030 under a range of electrification assumptions. The debate is not whether a deficit is coming, but how large it will be and whether recycling and substitution can fill part of the gap.

Copper recycling — which already accounts for roughly 30–35% of global supply — is expanding, but only gradually. Substituting aluminum for copper in some applications (particularly overhead transmission lines) is possible but involves trade-offs in efficiency and weight. Neither recycling nor substitution is likely to close the gap entirely during this decade.

The seasonal window: November through February

Overlaid on the structural story is a seasonal one. Historically, copper has shown its best price performance during the November-to-February window. The pattern is driven by a combination of factors: restocking demand ahead of Chinese New Year, when factories shut down and buyers stock up beforehand; the start of construction seasons in the Northern Hemisphere; and fiscal year-end and year-start activity among large industrial buyers.

Commodity analysts at Barchart and elsewhere have highlighted this Nov–Feb period as a historically proven seasonal play in copper, independent of the fundamental story. With Q4 2026 now underway, that seasonal tailwind is beginning to come into view — and it arrives against a backdrop of real underlying supply tightness rather than just calendar positioning.

This does not mean copper will necessarily rise through year-end. Macro headwinds — a stronger U.S. dollar, concerns about Chinese economic growth, or a broad commodities risk-off — can override seasonal patterns. But all else equal, the seasonal tendency adds to the already constructive case that Goldman Sachs and others are making for copper in the near term.

What the gold-copper ratio is signalling right now

One lens worth keeping in mind is the gold-copper ratio — the number of pounds (or tonnes) of copper that one ounce of gold can buy. This ratio is widely used as an economic barometer: gold is a safe haven, copper is a growth metal, and the ratio between them captures market expectations about the economic environment.

When the ratio is elevated — gold expensive relative to copper — it tends to coincide with periods of economic anxiety, when investors are buying gold for safety while copper demand is soft. When the ratio falls — copper strengthening relative to gold — it typically reflects confidence in global growth and industrial activity. GoldAlert tracks the gold-copper ratio live on its Market Ratios page, alongside the gold-silver, gold-oil and gold-platinum ratios.

A falling gold-copper ratio in a period where gold itself remains near all-time highs — as has been the case for much of 2026 — would be a particularly interesting signal: it would mean copper is outpacing even a gold price already elevated by central bank demand and geopolitical anxiety. That kind of cross-asset signal is worth watching as Q4 unfolds.

What copper's move means for precious metals investors

Copper and gold do not move in lockstep, but the copper market sends signals that are relevant even to investors whose primary interest is in gold and silver.

First, a genuinely tight copper market supports a broader commodities narrative. If real industrial demand is strong enough to push copper to multi-year highs despite a strong dollar and elevated interest rates, it suggests underlying global economic activity is more resilient than the bond market's recession fears imply. That is a mixed signal for gold: less safe-haven premium needed, but more underlying commodity demand that can keep inflation sticky and central banks cautious about cutting rates too far.

Second, copper's structural story is a reminder that supply constraints are not unique to precious metals. The same permitting timelines, geological challenges and capital intensity that make new gold and silver mines slow to develop apply to copper as well. If you believe in the commodity supercycle thesis — that a decade of under-investment in mining capacity is about to meet a decade of accelerating demand — copper is perhaps the single most compelling illustration of it.

Third, mining companies that produce copper alongside gold and silver — which describes many of the world's largest diversified miners — will see their earnings reflect copper's strength. Investors in gold mining ETFs should be aware that their funds may hold significant copper exposure through these diversified producers.
